 % Paper labels sec:ld-verifier and sec:ld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
 \label{sec:ld-verifier}
 \label{sec:ld-game}
 
 The classical low individual degree game is a two-player game based on the low individual degree variant of the multilinearity test of Babai, Fortnow, and Lund. In the basic version, one player (the ``points player'') receives a uniformly random point $u \in \F_q^m$ and answers with a value $a \in \F_q$, while the other player (the ``lines player'') receives a random line through $u$ --- either axis-parallel or diagonal --- and answers with a univariate polynomial describing the restriction of a global function to that line.  The Pauli basis test is the quantum low individual degree test of Natarajan and Vidick, in the slightly modified form introduced by Natarajan and Wright~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Informally, the test certifies that the players share the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, where $M = 2^m$. On a question of type $(\mathsf{Pauli}, W)$ with $W \in \{X,Z\}$, a player is expected to measure the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} and report the outcome $h$. Most subtests probe limited information about $h$: given a point $u_W \in \F_q^m$, a player is expected to report the evaluation $g_h(u_W)$ of the low-degree encoding $g_h$ of $h$, and for a fixed basis $W$ these probes are checked against each other by the classical low individual degree game of Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}. Consistency \emph{between} the two bases is checked through two-outcome probes: given additionally $r_W \in \F_q$, a player reports $\tr(g_h(u_W)\, r_W) \in \F_2$. The two binary measurements obtained in this way for $W = X$ and $W = Z$ either commute or anticommute, according to the value $\gamma \in \F_2$ of Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value} below. When $\gamma = 0$ the verifier checks commutation directly by asking for both bits simultaneously; when $\gamma = 1$ the verifier checks anticommutation by playing the Magic Square game, using Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.

   969	      \label{sec:apply-ldt}
   970	      In the previous section we showed how to combine the
   971	      approximately commuting $X$ and $Z$ basis point and line
   972	      measurements into a joint point measurement and a joint line
   973	      measurement. In this section we show how these measurements can be combined
   974				in a single measurement

   976	      $Z$-basis information, respectively, by applying the lemma that states quantum soundness of the classical low-degree test, Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}.
   977				
   978	      Introduce a ``combining'' map that
   979	      takes two polynomials $f, g \in \ideg_{d,m}(\F_q)$ and returns a new polynomial $\combine_{f,g} \in \ideg_{d,
   980	        2m+2}(\F_q)$ defined by
   981	      \[ \combine_{f,g}(\underbrace{x}_{\in \F_q^{m}},
   982	        \underbrace{z}_{\in \F_q^m}, \underbrace{\alpha}_{\in \F_q},
   983	        \underbrace{\beta}_{\in \F_q}) = \alpha f(x) + \beta g(z)\;. \]

Let $\line$ be a line in $\F_q^{2m+2}$ with intercept $u = (u_X, u_Z, u_\alpha, u_\beta)$ and slope $v = (v_X, v_Z, v_\alpha, v_\beta)$.    985	      \begin{equation}
   986	        \combine_{f,g}(u + t \cdot v) = (u_\alpha + t\cdot v_\alpha) f(u_X + t \cdot v_X) + (u_\beta + t \cdot v_\beta) g(u_Z + t \cdot v_Z)\;. \label{eq:combine-lines}

   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}

   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).

   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
   957	
   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}
   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.
   961	\end{definition}

   965	We now describe the question distribution of the game $\game^\pauli$, and show
   966	that it is a (typed) CL distribution.
   967	The question types in the game $\game^\pauli$ are

   969	  \label{eq:pauli-type}
   970	  \type^\pauli= \bigl( \{\Point, \ALine, \DLine, \Pauli, \Pair \} \times \{X,Z\} \bigr)

     9	This chapter completes the analysis of the Pauli basis test~\cite{Ji2020MIPStar}. Throughout, $(q,m,d)$ is an admissible parameter tuple (Definition~\ref{def:admissible}), $q = 2^t$, and $M = 2^m$ denotes the number of $q$-ary qudits tested for per player. (The letter $M$ also denotes measurement operators, always carrying super- and subscripts; the meaning is determined by context, as in the source.) We fix a projective strategy for the Pauli basis test game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{Pauli}}_{(q,m,d)}$ that succeeds with probability at least $1-\eps$, in the setting of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-observables}: the shared state $\ket{\psi}$ on registers $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$ is assumed padded with sufficiently many ancilla qubits in the state $\ket{0}$ (Definition~\ref{def:projective-strategy-setup}), and $\ket{\hat\psi}$ denotes the expanded state on the six registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''$, obtained by adjoining to each player the two halves of $M$ pairs $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}$ (Definition~\ref{def:expanded-state}). Unless stated otherwise, every $\approx_\delta$ and $\simeq_\delta$ statement below is taken with respect to the state $\ket{\hat\psi}$, over the question distribution named in the statement, with register placements indicated by subscripts; ``all symmetric equivalents'' refers to the register interchanges of Remark~\ref{def:symmetric-equivalents}.
    10	
    11	We use the following objects from the preceding chapters: the combined point projectors $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$ acting on the expanded space (Definition~\ref{def:expanded-point-measurement}); the projective polynomial-pair measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}, with outcomes pairs of polynomials in $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ and error function
    12	\[
    13		\delta_S(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a\bigl(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd}\bigr)
    14	\]
    15	for universal constants $a > 1$, $0 < b < 1$; the decoding map $\mathrm{Dec} = \mathrm{Dec}_{\F_q}\colon \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q) \to \F_q^{M}$ of the low-degree code (Definition~\ref{def:decoding-map}, applied with $H = \F_q$; see Remark~\ref{rem:qld-decoding-identity}), which maps a polynomial $g$ to the string of its evaluations on the hypercube $\{0,1\}^m$; and the low-degree encoding $h \mapsto g_h$ together with the vectors $\mathrm{ind}_m(u) \in \F_q^M$, characterized by $h \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g_h(u)$ for all $u \in \F_q^m$ \eqref{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}. Both maps are $\F_q$-linear, and $\mathrm{Dec}(g_h) = h$ for every $h \in \F_q^{M}$. We call a polynomial $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ an \emph{encoding} if $g = g_h$ for some $h \in \F_q^{M}$ or, equivalently, if $g$ is multilinear; since a multilinear polynomial is determined by its values on $\{0,1\}^m$, the encodings are exactly the $g$ with $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)} = g$, and
    16	\[
    17		\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g(u)
    18		\qquad \text{for every encoding $g$ and every } u \in \F_q^m\;.
    19	\]
    20	For a $g$ that is not an encoding the two sides of this identity are, as functions of $u$, distinct polynomials; see Remark~\ref{rem:qld-decoding-identity}.

    27	\begin{remark}[Choice of decoding map and the decoder--encoder identity]\label{rem:qld-decoding-identity}
    28		The source states the constructions of this chapter in terms of its boolean decoding map (the case $H = \{0,1\}$ of Definition~\ref{def:decoding-map}) while describing that map as returning the string of \emph{all} evaluations of $g$ on the hypercube. The proofs require the latter reading, $H = \F_q$, which is adopted throughout this chapter: the linearity of $\mathrm{Dec}$ and the identity $\mathrm{Dec}(g_h) = h$ for all $h \in \F_q^{M}$, both of which fail for the boolean map, are used in the symmetry step of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} and in the conjugation identity \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-6}. The source further asserts the identity $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g(u)$ for every $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$. Since the left-hand side equals $g_{\mathrm{Dec}(g)}(u)$, the identity holds exactly when $g$ is an encoding, and fails otherwise: for $m = 1$, $d \geq 2$, and $q > 2$, the polynomial $g(x) = x^2$ has $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_1(u) = u \neq u^2$. Accordingly, the proofs below invoke the identity only for encodings; in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} the contribution of the remaining outcomes is controlled by the bound \eqref{eq:qld-nonencoding-mass} on the mass that the measurement of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7} places on polynomials that are not encodings, while in the conjugation identity \eqref{eq:qld-unitary-6} the quantity $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u)$ cancels exactly.
    29	\end{remark}

    31	\section{The pulled-apart measurements and observables}
    32	
    33	The measurement $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ reads out an $X$-polynomial and a $Z$-polynomial simultaneously. We now separate the two readings again, this time as commuting actions on distinct registers: the polynomial outcome is measured on the players' original registers, while a genuine Pauli measurement acts on the EPR register $\mathrm{A}''$ (resp.\ $\mathrm{B}''$).
    34	
    35	\begin{definition}[Single-basis marginals of the polynomial-pair measurement]\label{def:s-w-marginals}
    36		\uses{lem:qld-4-7}
    37		Let $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ be the projective measurement of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}. For every $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ define
    38		\[
    39			\hat{S}^X_g = \sum_{g_Z} \hat{S}_{g,g_Z}
    40			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
    41			\hat{S}^Z_g = \sum_{g_X} \hat{S}_{g_X,g}\;,
    42		\]
    43		the sums ranging over $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$. Since $\{\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}\}$ is projective, its elements are mutually orthogonal projectors; hence each $\hat{S}^W_g$, for $W \in \{X,Z\}$, is a projector, and $\{\hat{S}^W_g\}_{g}$ is a projective measurement with outcomes in $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$.
    44	\end{definition}
    45	
    46	\begin{definition}[Pauli dot-product projectors]\label{def:tau-dot-product-projector}
    47		\uses{def:generalized-pauli}
    48		For $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $h \in \F_q^{M}$ let $\tau^W_h$ denote the projector corresponding to measuring $(\C^q)^{\ot M}$ in the $W$ basis and obtaining the outcome $h$ (Definition~\ref{def:generalized-pauli}). For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^{M}$, and $a \in \F_q$, define the projector
    49		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-tauwu}
    50			\tau^{W}_{a}(\tilde{u}) = \sum_{h \in \F_q^{M} \,:\, h \cdot \tilde{u} = a} \tau^W_{h}\;.
    51		\end{equation}
    52		For each fixed $\tilde{u}$, the family $\{\tau^W_a(\tilde{u})\}_{a \in \F_q}$ is a projective measurement on $(\C^q)^{\ot M}$.
    53	\end{definition}
    54	
    55	\begin{definition}[Pulled-apart Pauli basis measurements]\label{def:tilde-m-measurement}
    56		\uses{def:s-w-marginals, def:tau-dot-product-projector, def:decoding-map}
    57		For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^{M}$ define the measurement $\{\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a\}_{a \in \F_q}$ by
    58		\begin{equation}\label{eq:tilde_M}
    59			\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a = \sum_{g} \hat{S}^W_g \ot \tau_{(\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \tilde{u}) - a}^W(\tilde{u})\;,
    60		\end{equation}
    61		the sum ranging over $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$. If $\hat{S}^W_g$ is viewed as an operator acting on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'$ (resp.\ $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'$), then $\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a$ acts on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''$ (resp.\ $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''$), the $\tau^W$ factor acting on $\mathrm{A}''$ (resp.\ $\mathrm{B}''$). Each family $\{\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a\}_{a \in \F_q}$ is a projective measurement, because the $\hat{S}^W_g$ and the $\tau^W$ projectors are projective and, for each $g$, the projectors $\tau^W_{(\mathrm{Dec}(g)\cdot\tilde{u})-a}(\tilde{u})$ sum to the identity as $a$ ranges over $\F_q$.
    62	\end{definition}
    63	
    64	\begin{definition}[Pulled-apart Pauli observables]\label{def:tilde-w-observables}
    65		\uses{def:tilde-m-measurement, def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis, def:subfield-trace}
    66		Let $\{e_j\}_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}}$ be the self-dual basis for $\F_q$ over $\F_2$ of Definition~\ref{def:dual-self-dual-normal-basis}, and let $\tr = \tr_{q \to 2} \colon \F_q \to \F_2$ be the subfield trace. For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^M$, and $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$ define the operator
    67		\begin{equation}\label{eq:def-tildewj}
    68			\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) = \sum_{a \in \F_q} (-1)^{\tr(e_j a)} \, \tilde{M}_a^{W,\tilde{u}}\;,
    69		\end{equation}
    70		acting on the same registers as $\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a$.
    71	\end{definition}
    72	
    73	% In the source the following properties are stated inline with the
    74	% definition of the observables; they are recorded here as a lemma.
    75	\begin{lemma}[Product form and Pauli relations of the pulled-apart observables]\label{lem:tildew-product-form}
    76		\uses{def:tilde-w-observables, def:s-w-marginals, def:generalized-pauli, def:decoding-map, lem:qld-4-7}
    77		Let $\tau^W(\cdot)$ denote the generalized Pauli $W$ observable (Definition~\ref{def:generalized-pauli}). For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^M$, and $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$,
    78		\begin{equation}\label{eq:tildewj-product-form}
    79			\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})
    80			= \Big( \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (-1)^{\tr(e_j (\mathrm{Dec}(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} \, \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z} \Big) \ot \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u})\;,
    81		\end{equation}
    82		where $g_W$ denotes $g_X$ if $W = X$ and $g_Z$ if $W = Z$. In particular each $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ is Hermitian and squares to the identity. Moreover, the pulled-apart observables satisfy exactly the twisted commutation relations of the generalized Pauli observables $\tau^X(e_j \tilde{u})$ and $\tau^Z(e_{j'} \tilde{v})$: for all $j,j' \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$ and $\tilde{u},\tilde{v} \in \F_q^M$,
    83		\begin{equation}\label{eq:tildew-twisted-commutation}
    84			\tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u})\, \tilde{Z}^{j'}(\tilde{v})
    85			= (-1)^{\tr((e_j \tilde{u}) \cdot (e_{j'} \tilde{v}))}\, \tilde{Z}^{j'}(\tilde{v})\, \tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u})\;,
    86		\end{equation}
    87		where $\tr((e_j \tilde{u}) \cdot (e_{j'} \tilde{v})) = \tr(e_j e_{j'} (\tilde{u} \cdot \tilde{v}))$.
    88	\end{lemma}
    89	\begin{proof}
    90		\uses{def:tilde-m-measurement, def:tau-dot-product-projector, def:s-w-marginals, lem:pauli-observable-expansion, lem:twisted-commutation, lem:qld-4-7}
    91		Expanding $\tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) = \sum_{h} (-1)^{\tr(e_j (\tilde{u} \cdot h))}\, \tau^W_h$ on the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:tildewj-product-form} (Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-observable-expansion}), grouping the $h$ according to the value $a' = h \cdot \tilde{u}$ into the projectors $\tau^W_{a'}(\tilde{u})$ of \eqref{eq:def-tauwu}, collecting the pairs $(g_X,g_Z)$ with a common value $g_W = g$ into $\hat{S}^W_g$ (Definition~\ref{def:s-w-marginals}), and changing the summation variable to $a = (\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \tilde{u}) - a'$ recovers, by \eqref{eq:tilde_M} and \eqref{eq:def-tildewj}, the operator $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$; this proves \eqref{eq:tildewj-product-form}. Since the $\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}$ are mutually orthogonal projectors summing to the identity (Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}) and $\tau^W(e_j \tilde{u})$ is a Hermitian involution, the product form exhibits $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ as Hermitian with square $\sum_{g_X,g_Z} \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z} \ot \Id = \Id$. For \eqref{eq:tildew-twisted-commutation}, the two sign-weighted sums of the projectors $\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}$ appearing in the product forms of $\tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u})$ and $\tilde{Z}^{j'}(\tilde{v})$ commute with each other, so the commutation phase is that of $\tau^X(e_j \tilde{u})$ and $\tau^Z(e_{j'} \tilde{v})$, which is $(-1)^{\tr((e_j \tilde{u}) \cdot (e_{j'} \tilde{v}))}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:twisted-commutation}.
    92	\end{proof}

    97	\begin{remark}[The commutation phase across basis indices]\label{rem:qld-cross-phase}
    98		For $j \neq j'$ the source asserts that $\tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u})$ and $\tilde{Z}^{j'}(\tilde{v})$ commute for all $\tilde{u}, \tilde{v} \in \F_q^M$. Since $e_j e_{j'} \neq 0$ and the bilinear form $(a,b) \mapsto \tr(ab)$ on $\F_q$ is nondegenerate, there exist $\tilde{u}, \tilde{v}$ with $\tr(e_j e_{j'} (\tilde{u} \cdot \tilde{v})) = 1$, and for these \eqref{eq:tildew-twisted-commutation} yields anticommutation instead. By self-duality of the basis $\{e_j\}$, the dichotomy asserted by the source --- commutation for $j \neq j'$, and the phase $(-1)^{\tr((e_j\tilde{u}) \cdot (e_j\tilde{v}))}$ for $j = j'$ --- agrees with \eqref{eq:tildew-twisted-commutation} whenever $\tilde{u} \cdot \tilde{v} \in \{0,1\}$, in particular for all $\tilde{u}, \tilde{v} \in \{0,1\}^M$. The relations \eqref{eq:tildew-twisted-commutation} are not used in the remainder of the chapter.
    99	\end{remark}

   573			$((\ell_X, u_X), (\ell_Z, z'))$, where $z'$ is a uniformly random
   574			point of $\ell_Z$ sampled independently of $u$, is distributed
   575			according to $D_{\mathrm{v},i} \times D_{\mathrm{v},j}$, and
   576			symmetrically the pair $((\ell_X, x'), (\ell_Z, u_Z))$, with $x'$
   577			a uniformly random point of $\ell_X$ sampled independently of
   578			$u$, is distributed according to
   579			$D_{\mathrm{v},i} \times D_{\mathrm{v},j}$. (No assertion is made
   580			about the joint conditional law of the pair $(u_X, u_Z)$.)
   581			\item If $\ell$ is axis-parallel, then $\ell_X$ and $\ell_Z$ are
   582			axis-parallel.
   583		\end{enumerate}
   584		(Property~3 is not part of the numbered statement in the source; see
   585		Remark~\ref{rem:qld-sublines-property-three}.)
   586	\end{lemma}
   587	\begin{proof}
   588		\uses{def:line-representative, def:ld-question-distribution,
   589			def:line-point-dist, def:ith-restricted-line, def:line,
   590			prop:line-equiv}
   591		The distribution $D$ is described by a sampling procedure. First sample
   592		$(\ell, u)$ from the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and write
   593		$u = (u_X, u_Z, \alpha, \beta)$, so that Property~1 holds by
   594		construction; all auxiliary randomness introduced below is sampled
   595		independently of $(\ell, u)$. We write $\chi$ for the index function of
   596		Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} at dimension $m$, whose
   597		classes $\chi^{-1}(i)$ for $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ partition $\F_q$
   598		into sets of equal size $q/m$, and $\chi_{2m+2}$ for the index function
   599		at dimension $2m+2$, defined because $2m+2$ divides $q$. By a
   600		\emph{fresh diagonal direction pair} we mean a pair $(s', w')$ with
   601		$s'$ uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $w' \in \F_q^m$ having coordinates
   602		$1, \dots, \chi(s')-1$ equal to $0$ and the remaining coordinates
   603		uniformly random; this is exactly the law of the coordinate--direction
   604		data of the diagonal component of the line-point distribution over
   605		$\F_q^m$ (Definition~\ref{def:line-point-dist}).
   606	
   607		If $\ell$ is axis-parallel, $\ell = (v, e_j)$ with
   608		$v = (v_X, v_Z, \alpha_0, \beta_0)$ and $j \in \{1, \dots, 2m+2\}$, set
   609		$\ell_X = (v'_X, e_{i_X})$ and $\ell_Z = (v'_Z, e_{i_Z})$ where: for
   610		$1 \le j \le m$, $i_X = j$ and $i_Z$ is uniformly random in
   611		$\{1,\dots,m\}$; for $m+1 \le j \le 2m$, $i_X$ is uniformly random and
   612		$i_Z = j - m$; for $2m+1 \le j \le 2m+2$, both $i_X$ and $i_Z$ are
   613		uniformly random; and $v'_X, v'_Z$ are the canonical line
   614		representatives of $v_X, v_Z$ for the chosen directions
   615		(Definition~\ref{def:line-representative}), so that $v_X \in \ell_X$
   616		and $v_Z \in \ell_Z$.
   617	
   618		If $\ell$ is diagonal, $\ell = (v, s, w)$, then by the construction of
   619		the diagonal component of the line-point distribution
   620		(Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} instantiated at
   621		dimension $2m+2$) the direction $w = (w_X, w_Z, \gamma, \delta)$ has
   622		coordinates $1, \dots, j-1$ equal to $0$, where $j = \chi_{2m+2}(s)$,
   623		and its remaining coordinates are uniformly random. These remaining
   624		coordinates may also vanish, so $w$ need not have a nonzero coordinate
   625		at index $j$ and may be the zero vector, in which case $\ell$ is a
   626		singleton (Definition~\ref{def:line}).
   627		% The source proof describes w as "a direction vector whose first
   628		% nonzero coordinate is j = chi(s)"
   629		% (references/qpbt-paper/14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex, proof
   630		% of lem:qld-sublines); the distribution delivers only the weaker
   631		% property recorded here, which is the one the argument uses. The
   632		% source also leaves the laws of s_X and s_Z unspecified ("chosen such
   633		% that chi(s_X) = j"); the uniform choices below are needed for the
   634		% exact marginals claimed in Property 2.
   635		Sample $\ell_X = (v'_X, s_X, w'_X)$ and $\ell_Z = (v'_Z, s_Z, w'_Z)$
   636		where: for $1 \le j \le m$, $w'_X = w_X$ and $w'_Z = w_Z$, with $s_X$
   637		uniformly random in the class $\chi^{-1}(j)$ and $s_Z$ uniformly
   638		random in the class $\chi^{-1}(1)$; for $m+1 \le j \le 2m$, the pair
   639		$(s_X, w'_X)$ is a fresh diagonal direction pair and $w'_Z = w_Z$,
   640		with $s_Z$ uniformly random in the class $\chi^{-1}(j-m)$; for
   641		$2m+1 \le j \le 2m+2$, both $(s_X, w'_X)$ and $(s_Z, w'_Z)$ are fresh
   642		diagonal direction pairs, sampled independently; and $v'_X, v'_Z$ are
   643		the canonical representatives of $v_X, v_Z$ for the directions
   644		$w'_X, w'_Z$.
   645	
   646		Property~3 is immediate from the procedure: when $\ell$ is
   647		axis-parallel, both $\ell_X$ and $\ell_Z$ are constructed to be
   648		axis-parallel. The containments in Property~2 hold for every point
   649		$u^\dagger = (u^\dagger_X, u^\dagger_Z, \alpha^\dagger,
   650		\beta^\dagger)$ of $\ell$: the block $u^\dagger_X$ differs from $v_X$
   651		by a multiple of the direction of $\ell_X$ when that direction is
   652		inherited from $\ell$ (namely $e_j$ for axis-parallel $\ell$ with
   653		$1 \le j \le m$, and $w_X$ for diagonal $\ell$ with $1 \le j \le m$),
   654		and equals $v_X$ in all other cases, since then the corresponding
   655		block of the direction of $\ell$ vanishes; in either case
   656		$u^\dagger_X \in \ell_X$ because $v_X \in \ell_X$, and symmetrically
   657		$u^\dagger_Z \in \ell_Z$.
   658	
   659		For the distributional part of Property~2, observe first that
   660		$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$ is a function of $\ell$ and of the auxiliary
   661		randomness alone: the directions used are either read off from the
   662		direction data of $\ell$ or freshly sampled, and by
   663		Proposition~\ref{prop:line-equiv} the canonical representatives
   664		$v'_X, v'_Z$ do not depend on which base point of $\ell$ is used to
   665		compute them. Under both components of the line-point distribution the
   666		point $u$ is uniformly distributed on $\F_q^{2m+2}$ and, conditioned
   667		on the line $\ell$, uniformly distributed on the points of $\ell$
   668		(each of the $q$ values of the line parameter, or the single point
   669		when the direction vanishes, being equally likely). Hence, conditioned
   670		on $(\ell, \ell_X, \ell_Z)$, the sampled point $u$ is uniformly
   671		distributed on $\ell$, and it suffices to establish the claimed
   672		mixture description for the tuple $(\ell_X, \ell_Z, u)$ produced by
   673		the procedure itself.
   674	
   675		Condition on the component of the line-point distribution
   676		(axis-parallel or diagonal) and on $j$; the mixture of Property~2 is
   677		over these choices together with the fresh index choices, and the
   678		blocks $u_X, u_Z$ of $u$ are independent and uniform on $\F_q^m$,
   679		independent of all direction data. In the axis-parallel case with
   680		$1 \le j \le m$, the pair $(\ell_X, u_X)$ consists of the uniformly
   681		random point $u_X$ together with the canonical axis-parallel line
   682		through it in direction $e_j$, so
   683		$(\ell_X, u_X) \sim D_{\mathrm{ALine},j}$, while, conditioned
   684		additionally on $i_Z$, the pair $(\ell_Z, u_Z)$ consists of the
   685		uniformly random point $u_Z$ together with the canonical line through
   686		it in direction $e_{i_Z}$, so
   687		$(\ell_Z, u_Z) \sim D_{\mathrm{ALine},i_Z}$; the two pairs are
   688		functions of the disjoint independent data $u_X$ and $(u_Z, i_Z)$,
   689		hence independent. In the diagonal case with $1 \le j \le m$, the
   690		triple $(u_X, w_X, s_X)$ has $u_X$ uniform, $w_X$ with coordinates
   691		$1, \dots, j-1$ equal to $0$ and the remaining coordinates uniform,
   692		and $s_X$ uniform in $\chi^{-1}(j)$, which is exactly the law
   693		generating $D_{\mathrm{DLine},j}$; hence
   694		$(\ell_X, u_X) \sim D_{\mathrm{DLine},j}$, and similarly
   695		$(\ell_Z, u_Z) \sim D_{\mathrm{DLine},1}$ since $w_Z$ is uniform and
   696		$s_Z$ is uniform in $\chi^{-1}(1)$; the two pairs are functions of the
   697		disjoint independent data $(u_X, w_X, s_X)$ and $(u_Z, w_Z, s_Z)$,
   698		hence independent. The remaining cases are analogous: each of
   699		$(\ell_X, u_X)$ and $(\ell_Z, u_Z)$ is either built from the inherited
   700		direction block as above, or from a fresh axis index or fresh diagonal
   701		direction pair, in which case it is distributed as the uniform mixture
   702		over $i$ of $D_{\mathrm{v},i}$ for the corresponding type
   703		$\mathrm{v}$; and the two pairs are always functions of disjoint
   704		independent collections of the variables $u_X$, $u_Z$, the direction
   705		blocks, and the fresh auxiliary choices, hence independent conditioned
   706		on the component. Within each component this yields exactly the
   707		description of Property~2: the pair $(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$ is
   708		product-distributed according to the line marginals of
   709		$D_{\mathrm{v},i}$ and $D_{\mathrm{v},j}$, and, conditioned on
   710		$(\ell_X, \ell_Z)$, each of $u_X$ and $u_Z$ is uniformly distributed
   711		on its line, because under each restricted distribution the point is
   712		uniform on the line conditionally on the line. The equivalent product
   713		formulations follow from the same conditional uniformity.
   714	\end{proof}

   734	\begin{lemma}[Replacing the combined point measurement by the ordered product]
   735		\label{lem:claim-17-1}
   736		% claim:17-1 in the paper; the original label is recorded here as a
   737		% comment for cross-reference fidelity.
   738		\uses{lem:qld-sublines, lem:qld-xz-lines, lem:qld-4-10,
   739			def:expanded-point-measurement, def:expanded-state}
   740		\begin{align*}
   741			\E_{(\ell,\ell_X,\ell_Z) \sim D}\
   742			\E_{(x,z,\alpha,\beta) \in \ell}
   743			&\sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
   744			\big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
   745			\big(\hat{Q}^{x,z}_{f_X(x),f_Z(z)}\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}
   746			\ket{\hat\psi} \\
   747			\approx_{\delta_Q^{1/2}}\
   748			\E_{(\ell,\ell_X,\ell_Z) \sim D}\
   749			\E_{(x,z,\alpha,\beta) \in \ell}
   750			&\sum_{f_X,f_Z} \bra{\hat\psi}
   751			\big(T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z}\big)_{\mathsf{A}\mathsf{A}'} \ot
   752			\big(\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{f_Z(z)} \,
   753			\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{f_X(x)}
   754			\big)_{\mathsf{B}\mathsf{A}''}
   755			\ket{\hat\psi}\,.
   756		\end{align*}
   757	\end{lemma}
   758	\begin{proof}
   759		\uses{lem:qld-4-10, lem:qld-sublines, lem:qld-xz-lines,
   760			def:line-point-dist}
   761		Write
   762		$W^{x,z}_{a,b} = \hat{Q}^{x,z}_{a,b}
   763		- \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},Z),z}_{b}
   764		\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},X),x}_{a}$
   765		and apply the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality to the difference of the two
   766		sides. The first factor is at most $1$ because
   767		$\sum_{f_X,f_Z \,:\, f_X(x)=a,\ f_Z(z)=b}
   768		T^{\ell_X,\ell_Z}_{f_X,f_Z} \le \Id$
   769		for every $x, z, a, b$. For the second factor, note that when $\ell$ is
   770		drawn from the line-point distribution over $\F_q^{2m+2}$, a uniformly
   771		random point $(x,z,\alpha,\beta)$ on $\ell$ is a uniformly random point
   772		of $\F_q^{2m+2}$, so the coordinates $x, z$ are independent and uniform
   773		in $\F_q^m$; hence
   774		$\E_{x,z} \sum_{a,b}
   775		\bra{\hat\psi} \Id \ot (W^{x,z}_{a,b})^2 \ket{\hat\psi}
   776		\le \delta_Q$
   777		by \eqref{eq:qld-q-cons-m-hat-zx}. The total error is therefore at most
   778		$\sqrt{\delta_Q}$.
   779	\end{proof}

   252	\section{The Pauli basis test}
   253	% Paper label sec:qld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   254	\label{sec:qld-game}
   255	
   256	The Pauli basis test is the quantum low individual degree test of Natarajan and Vidick, in the slightly modified form introduced by Natarajan and Wright~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Informally, the test certifies that the players share the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, where $M = 2^m$. On a question of type $(\mathsf{Pauli}, W)$ with $W \in \{X,Z\}$, a player is expected to measure the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} and report the outcome $h$. Most subtests probe limited information about $h$: given a point $u_W \in \F_q^m$, a player is expected to report the evaluation $g_h(u_W)$ of the low-degree encoding $g_h$ of $h$, and for a fixed basis $W$ these probes are checked against each other by the classical low individual degree game of Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}. Consistency \emph{between} the two bases is checked through two-outcome probes: given additionally $r_W \in \F_q$, a player reports $\tr(g_h(u_W)\, r_W) \in \F_2$. The two binary measurements obtained in this way for $W = X$ and $W = Z$ either commute or anticommute, according to the value $\gamma \in \F_2$ of Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value} below. When $\gamma = 0$ the verifier checks commutation directly by asking for both bits simultaneously; when $\gamma = 1$ the verifier checks anticommutation by playing the Magic Square game, using Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:108:	The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\ell(u_0, 0) = \{u_0\}$, every $t \in \F_q$ satisfies $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, and the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} shows that any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount, which is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.
blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:115:	Let $\polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ denote the set of POVM measurements indexed by $\polyfunc{m}{q}{d}$, the polynomial representatives of individual degree at most $d$ in each variable; this is the notion of Definition~\ref{def:polymeasurements}, and the argument order $(m,q,d)$ follows that definition (the paper orders the arguments as $(m,d,q)$). By Definition~\ref{def:polynomials-degree}, evaluation identifies these representatives with the corresponding polynomial functions $g\colon \F_q^m \to \F_q$, bijectively whenever $d \le q-1$; the parameter regimes of this chapter (Definition~\ref{def:introparams} fixes $d = 1$, and admissibility gives $q \ge 2$) always satisfy this. More generally, for an integer $k$ and tuples $m = (m_1,\ldots,m_k)$, $q = (q_1,\ldots,q_k)$, $d = (d_1,\ldots,d_k)$, let $\mathrm{PolyMeas}(m,q,d,k)$ denote the set of measurements $G = \{G_{g_1,\ldots,g_k}\}$ such that for each $i \in \{1,\ldots,k\}$, the outcome index $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i\colon \F_{q_i}^{m_i} \to \F_{q_i}$ of individual degree at most $d_i$.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:164:	The two-prover tensor-code test for the code $\code^{\ot m}$, as described in Figures~1 and~2 of~\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, agrees with the game $\mathcal G^{\mathrm{ld}}$ with parameters $\mathsf{ldparams}$ and $k=1$ on every question pair whose diagonal-line direction is nonzero: the axis-parallel line-versus-point test is their axis-parallel lines test, with the roles of the two players chosen uniformly at random, which is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor-code test from Section~4.1 there; the diagonal line-versus-point test is their subcube commutation test, again with the added symmetrization between the players; and the consistency test is their synchronicity test. On diagonal line-versus-point questions with direction $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$, the win predicate of Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} resolves an ambiguity of the source (Remark~\ref{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}), and the resolution is not required to match the acceptance convention of the subcube commutation test on this event: the event has probability at most $2/(mq)$ under the question distribution, since the direction $\pi_{i-1}(v)$ vanishes with probability $\frac1m \sum_{j=1}^m q^{-j} \le \frac{1}{m(q-1)} \le \frac{2}{mq}$ over uniform $(s,v)$, so the success probabilities of any fixed strategy in the two games differ by at most $2/(mq)$. A projective strategy that succeeds in $\mathcal G^{\mathrm{ld}}$ with probability at least $1-\eps$ therefore succeeds in the tensor-code test with probability at least $1 - \eps - 2/(mq)$. Theorem~4.7 of~\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, instantiated with its internal parameter $k$ chosen as $m^3 d$ (this parameter is unrelated to the simultaneity parameter $k$ of $\mathsf{ldparams}$) and applied with the success deficit $\eps + 2/(mq)$ in place of $\eps$, then yields the present statement for $k = 1$: since $0 < b \le 1$ and $m \ge 1$ give $(\eps + 2/(mq))^b \le \eps^b + 2\,q^{-b}$, the additional error is absorbed into $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$ by enlarging the universal constant $a$, using $dmk \ge 1$. The case of general $k$ follows by a standard reduction, following exactly the derivation of Theorem~4.43 from Theorem~4.40 in~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Quantum soundness of the low individual degree test itself is the result of~\cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}; Remark~\ref{rem:ld-soundness-provider} relates the present statement to Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal}, which proves that result.
blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:168:	Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} is imported: the proof above reduces it to Theorem~4.7 of~\cite{Ji2021Quantum}, instantiated with its internal parameter $k$ chosen as $m^3 d$, followed by the extension to simultaneous $k$-tuples of~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. The result of~\cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree} that underlies it is proved here as Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal}: for every projective strategy passing the $(m,q,d)$ low individual degree test of Definition~\ref{def:low-individual-degree-test} with probability at least $1-\eps$, that theorem produces measurements in $\polymeas{m}{q}{d}$ satisfying consistency relations of the same shape as the three approximations of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness}. Neither implication is proved in this chapter, and the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} given above does not invoke Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal}.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch12_qpbt_games.tex:53:	The symmetrization argument of Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetric-strat} below invokes Naimark dilation in the form of Theorem~\ref{thm:naimark} (stated and proved in Chapter~\ref{chap:projective}): a bipartite state together with two sub-measurement families can be replaced, without changing any of the correlations $\bra{\psi} A^x_a \ot B^y_b \ket{\psi}$, by a product-extended state together with projective sub-measurements on the enlarged spaces. When the input families are complete measurements, the dilated projective sub-measurements can be completed by assigning the residual projector of each family to one fixed outcome; the resulting projective measurements reproduce the same correlations on the extended state, since the correlation-preservation identity forces the extended state to lie in the range of the total projector of each dilated family. This completed form, with genuinely projective measurements, is the one used in Lemma~\ref{lem:symmetric-strat}; for the proof the source refers to Theorem 5.1 of \cite{Ji2020LowIndividualDegree}, which is stated for complete measurements. The source follows its statement of the dilation theorem with a sentence announcing an ``orthogonalization lemma'' from the literature that is never actually stated there; nothing in this chapter depends on it.

    97	\begin{remark}[The commutation phase across basis indices]\label{rem:qld-cross-phase}
    98		For $j \neq j'$ the source asserts that $\tilde{X}^j(\tilde{u})$ and $\tilde{Z}^{j'}(\tilde{v})$ commute for all $\tilde{u}, \tilde{v} \in \F_q^M$. Since $e_j e_{j'} \neq 0$ and the bilinear form $(a,b) \mapsto \tr(ab)$ on $\F_q$ is nondegenerate, there exist $\tilde{u}, \tilde{v}$ with $\tr(e_j e_{j'} (\tilde{u} \cdot \tilde{v})) = 1$, and for these \eqref{eq:tildew-twisted-commutation} yields anticommutation instead. By self-duality of the basis $\{e_j\}$, the dichotomy asserted by the source --- commutation for $j \neq j'$, and the phase $(-1)^{\tr((e_j\tilde{u}) \cdot (e_j\tilde{v}))}$ for $j = j'$ --- agrees with \eqref{eq:tildew-twisted-commutation} whenever $\tilde{u} \cdot \tilde{v} \in \{0,1\}$, in particular for all $\tilde{u}, \tilde{v} \in \{0,1\}^M$. The relations \eqref{eq:tildew-twisted-commutation} are not used in the remainder of the chapter.
    99	\end{remark}

   101	\section{Consistency with the points measurements}
   102	
   103	The next lemma shows that the pulled-apart measurements are consistent with the original points measurements of the strategy, and self-consistent. In its statement, and for the remainder of the chapter, $\delta_S$ denotes the function of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}, enlarged by an adjustment of the universal constants $a$ and $b$ so as to also dominate additional error terms of order $\sqrt{\eps}$, $\eps$, and $md/q$ that the source absorbs into $\delta_S$ along the way; such an adjustment is possible since, after shrinking $b$ to at most $1/2$, the term $\eps^b$ dominates $\sqrt{\eps}$ and $\eps$ for $\eps \leq 1$, while $(md)^a q^{-b}$ dominates $md/q$.
   104	
   105	\begin{lemma}[Consistency and self-consistency of the pulled-apart measurements]\label{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis}
   106		\uses{def:tilde-m-measurement, def:tilde-w-observables, def:projective-strategy-setup, def:expanded-state, def:consistency, def:povm-distance, lem:qld-4-7, def:indicator-vector}
   107		The measurements $\{\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a\}_{a \in \F_q}$ and observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ satisfy the following properties.
   108		% The paper's statement also quantifies item 1 over j, but j does not occur
   109		% in item 1; the vacuous quantifier is dropped here.
   110		\begin{enumerate}
   111			\item (\textbf{Consistency with points measurements}) For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, on average over uniformly random $u \in \F_q^m$,
   112			\[
   113				\Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''} \ot \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a \simeq_{\delta_S} M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a \ot \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''}
   114			\]
   115			and
   116			\[
   117				\tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a \ot \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''} \simeq_{\delta_S} \Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''} \ot M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a\;,
   118			\]
   119			with the answer summation over $a \in \F_q$.
   120			\item (\textbf{Self-consistency}) For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$, on average over uniformly random $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^{M}$,
   121			\[
   122				\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \ot \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''} \approx_{\delta_S} \Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''} \ot \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})\;.
   123			\]
   124		\end{enumerate}
   125	\end{lemma}
   126	\begin{proof}
   127		\uses{lem:qld-4-7, lem:qld-constructing-the-paulis-helper, def:expanded-point-measurement, def:tilde-m-measurement, def:tau-dot-product-projector, def:decoding-map, def:indicator-vector, lem:qld-win-implications, lem:qld-comm-cons, fact:add-a-proj, fact:agreement, fact:triangle, fact:data-processing, def:bracket, lem:povm-to-obs, lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}
   128		% Support restriction added: the source (line 1492 of
   129		% 14_analysis_of_the_pauli_basis_test.tex) rewrites Dec(g).ind_m(u) as
   130		% g(u) for every outcome g; see Remark rem:qld-decoding-identity.
   131		We first bound the mass that the marginal measurements $\{\hat{S}^W_g\}$ place on polynomials that are not encodings. On average over uniformly random $u \in \F_q^m$, the point-consistency relation \eqref{eq:qld-s-point-con-bob} of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7} gives $(\hat{S}^W_{[g(u)=a]})_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \approx_{\delta_S} (\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a)_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{B}''}$ (Lemma~\ref{fact:agreement}); the consistency and Pauli-basis-consistency checks of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-win-implications} give, again on average over uniform $u$ and combining through Lemma~\ref{fact:data-processing}, Lemma~\ref{fact:agreement}, and Lemma~\ref{fact:triangle}, that $(M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_{a'})_{\mathrm{A}} \approx_{O(\eps)} (M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a']})_{\mathrm{A}}$; and replacing the point factor of the convolution form of $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$ (Definition~\ref{def:expanded-point-measurement}) accordingly costs the same error, because the projectors $\tau^W_{a''}(\mathrm{ind}_m(u))$ of \eqref{eq:def-tauwu} are mutually orthogonal (Lemma~\ref{fact:add-a-proj}). Writing
   132		\[
   133			K^u_a = \sum_{a' + a'' = a} \bigl(M^{(\mathrm{Pauli},W)}_{[g_h(u)=a']}\bigr)_{\mathrm{A}} \ot \bigl(\tau^W_{a''}(\mathrm{ind}_m(u))\bigr)_{\mathrm{B}''}\;,
   134		\]
   135		a projective measurement, Lemma~\ref{fact:triangle} and Lemma~\ref{fact:agreement} therefore give, using $\delta_S \geq \eps$,
   136		\[
   137			\E_{u \in \F_q^m} \sum_a \bra{\hat\psi} (\hat{S}^W_{[g(u)=a]})_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot (K^u_a)_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\hat\psi} \geq 1 - O(\delta_S)\;.
   138		\]
   139		Expanding $K^u_a$ over pairs $(h, h'')$ of Pauli outcomes, a term of the left-hand side with outcomes $(g, h, h'')$ is constrained by $g(u) = g_h(u) + g_{h''}(u) = g_{h + h''}(u)$, by the linearity of the encoding \eqref{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}. If $g$ is not an encoding then $g \neq g_{h+h''}$, and both are polynomials of total degree at most $md$, so the constraint holds for at most an $md/q$ fraction of $u$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}). Since all terms are nonnegative and, for each $g$, the operators of the $(h,h'')$-sum add up to the identity, it follows that
   140		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qld-nonencoding-mass}
   141			\sum_{g \,\text{not an encoding}} \bra{\hat\psi} (\hat{S}^W_g)_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ket{\hat\psi} \,\leq\, O(\delta_S) + \frac{md}{q} \,\leq\, O(\delta_S)\;,
   142		\end{equation}
   143		and symmetrically with the registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'$ in place of $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'$. (If $d = 0$, every element of $\mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$ is constant, hence an encoding, and the left-hand side vanishes.)
   144	
   145		For the first item, in the case where $M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$ acts on register $\mathrm{A}$ and $\tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a$ on $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''$, expanding \eqref{eq:tilde_M} and \eqref{eq:def-tauwu} and using the convolution form of the combined projectors $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$ (Definition~\ref{def:expanded-point-measurement}) gives the exact identity
   146		\[
   147			\E_{u \in \F_q^m} \sum_a \bra{\hat\psi} M^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a \ot \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a \ket{\hat\psi}
   148			= \E_{u \in \F_q^m} \sum_g \bra{\hat\psi} (\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_{\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u)})_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{B}''} \ot (\hat{S}^W_g)_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ket{\hat\psi}\;.
   149		\]
   150		For encodings $g$ the subscript $\mathrm{Dec}(g) \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u)$ equals $g(u)$; discarding the (nonnegative) terms with $g$ not an encoding and reinstating the corresponding terms with subscript $g(u)$, each of which is at most $\bra{\hat\psi} (\hat{S}^W_g)_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ket{\hat\psi}$, shows that the right-hand side is at least
   151		\[
   152			\E_{u \in \F_q^m} \sum_g \bra{\hat\psi} (\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_{g(u)})_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{B}''} \ot (\hat{S}^W_g)_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ket{\hat\psi} - O(\delta_S)
   153			\geq 1 - O(\delta_S)
   154		\]
   155		by \eqref{eq:qld-nonencoding-mass} and Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7}, and the register-interchanged relation follows analogously. For the second item one first shows that, on average over uniformly random $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^M$,
   156		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qld-pulling-cons}
   157			\bigl( \tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a \bigr)_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''} \approx_{\delta_S} \bigl( \tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a \bigr)_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''}\;:
   158		\end{equation}
   159		right-multiplying by the resolution $\sum_g (\hat{S}^W_g)_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ot (\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_{g(u)})_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{A}''} \approx_{\delta_S} \Id$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-constructing-the-paulis-helper} (with Lemma~\ref{fact:add-a-proj}) and expanding the products of $\tau^W$ projectors via \eqref{eq:def-tauwu} and $h \cdot \mathrm{ind}_m(u) = g_h(u)$ places $(\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a)_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''}$ within $O(\delta_S)$ of a sum over pairs $(g,h)$ with $(\mathrm{Dec}(g)-h)\cdot\tilde{u} = a$. One then applies, in turn, the self-consistency of the points measurements (Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-win-implications}) at cost $\eps$; the exact identity $\ket{\hat\psi} = \sum_{h'} (\tau^W_{h'})_{\mathrm{B}'} \ot (\tau^W_{h'})_{\mathrm{B}''} \ket{\hat\psi}$ of the EPR registers; Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-constructing-the-paulis-helper} twice more (once through a Cauchy--Schwarz detour of cost $O(\sqrt{\eps})$ using the self-consistency of the $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_a$, Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-comm-cons}); and finally a Schwartz--Zippel step (Lemma~\ref{lem:schwartz-zippel-total-degree}, for polynomials of total degree at most $md$) which replaces the event $(g'-g_{h'})(u) = (g-g_h)(u)$ by the polynomial identity $g'-g_{h'} = g-g_h$ at cost $md/q$. The resulting expression
   160		\[
   161			\sum_{\substack{g,h,g',h': \\ g' - g_{h'} = g - g_h \\ (\mathrm{Dec}(g)-h)\cdot \tilde{u} = a}}
   162			\Bigl((\hat{S}^W_g)_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ot (\tau_h^W)_{\mathrm{A}''} \Bigr) \cdot \Bigl( (\hat{S}^W_{g'})_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot (\tau_{h'}^W)_{\mathrm{B}''} \Bigr)
   163		\]
   164		is symmetric under exchanging $(g,h)$ with $(g',h')$: since $\mathrm{Dec}$ is linear with $\mathrm{Dec}(g_{h}) = h$ for all $h \in \F_q^M$ (Remark~\ref{rem:qld-decoding-identity}), the constraint $g' - g_{h'} = g - g_h$ implies $\mathrm{Dec}(g) - h = \mathrm{Dec}(g') - h'$, so the two constraint sets coincide. The same derivation therefore bounds the distance of the displayed expression to $(\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a)_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''}$, and \eqref{eq:qld-pulling-cons} follows after absorbing the error terms $O(\sqrt{\eps})$ and $O(md/q)$ into $\delta_S$. Finally, since $\{\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_a\}$ is projective, Item~2 of Lemma~\ref{fact:agreement}, data processing along the map $a \mapsto \tr(e_j a)$ (Lemma~\ref{fact:data-processing}), and Item~1 of Lemma~\ref{fact:agreement} yield $(\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_{[\tr(e_j \cdot) = b]})_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''} \approx_{\delta_S} (\tilde{M}^{W,\tilde{u}}_{[\tr(e_j \cdot) = b]})_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''}$ with answer summation over $b \in \F_2$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:povm-to-obs} converts this into the claimed self-consistency of the observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$.
   165	\end{proof}

   171	Lemmas~\ref{lem:qld-4-7} and~\ref{lem:qld-comm-cons} imply the following two estimates, which were used in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis}.

   173	\begin{lemma}[The marginals absorb the point measurements]\label{lem:qld-constructing-the-paulis-helper}
   174		\uses{def:s-w-marginals, def:expanded-point-measurement, def:expanded-state, def:povm-distance, lem:qld-4-7, def:symmetric-equivalents}
   175		For $W \in \{X,Z\}$, on average over uniformly random $u \in \F_q^m$,
   176		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qld-sg-cons}
   177			\sum_g (\hat{S}^W_g)_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ot (\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point},W),u}_{g(u)})_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{A}''} \approx_{\delta_S} \Id
   178		\end{equation}
   179		and
   180		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qld-sg-cons2}
   181			\bigl(\hat{S}^W_g \cdot (\Id - \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point}, W), u}_{g(u)})\bigr)_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \approx_{\delta_S} 0\;,
   182		\end{equation}
   183		where the answer summation is over $g \in \mathrm{ideg}_{d,m}(\F_q)$, and where in \eqref{eq:qld-sg-cons2} an additional error term of order $\eps$ is absorbed into $\delta_S$. Furthermore, all symmetric equivalents of these approximations also hold (Remark~\ref{def:symmetric-equivalents}).
   184	\end{lemma}
   185	\begin{proof}
   186		\uses{lem:qld-4-7, fact:agreement, fact:add-a-proj, def:bracket, lem:qld-comm-cons}
   187		The point-consistency conclusion of Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-4-7} states that, on average over $u \in \F_q^m$,
   188		\[
   189			\bra{\hat\psi} \sum_g (\hat{S}^W_g)_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ot (\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point}, W), u}_{g(u)})_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{A}''} \ket{\hat\psi} \geq 1 - \delta_S\;,
   190		\]
   191		which says exactly that the operator on the left-hand side of \eqref{eq:qld-sg-cons} is $\delta_S$-consistent with $\Id$; Lemma~\ref{fact:agreement} upgrades this $\simeq_{\delta_S}$ statement to the $\approx_{\delta_S}$ statement \eqref{eq:qld-sg-cons}. For \eqref{eq:qld-sg-cons2}, the same consistency, written with the coarse-graining $\hat{S}^W_{[g(u)=a]} = \sum_{g : g(u) = a} \hat{S}^W_g$ as $(\hat{S}^W_{[g(u)=a]})_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \approx_{\delta_S} (\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point}, W), u}_{a})_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{A}''}$ with answer summation over $a \in \F_q$, is left-multiplied by $(\hat{S}^W_{[g(u)=a]})_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'}$ using Lemma~\ref{fact:add-a-proj}; moving $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point}, W), u}_a$ from registers $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{A}''$ to $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'$ costs a further $\eps$ by Cauchy--Schwarz together with the self-consistency of the $\hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point}, W), u}_a$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:qld-comm-cons}), giving
   192		\[
   193			(\hat{S}^W_{[g(u)=a]})_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \approx_{O(\delta_S + \eps)} (\hat{S}^W_{[g(u)=a]} \cdot \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point}, W), u}_{a})_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'}\;.
   194		\]
   195		Expanding
   196		\[
   197			\E_u \sum_g \bigl\| (\hat{S}^W_{g} \cdot (\Id - \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point}, W), u}_{g(u)}))_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ket{\hat\psi} \bigr\|^2
   198			= \E_u \sum_a \bra{\hat\psi} \bigl((\Id - \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point}, W), u}_{a}) \cdot \hat{S}^W_{[g(u)=a]} \cdot (\Id - \hat{M}^{(\mathrm{Point}, W), u}_{a})\bigr)_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ket{\hat\psi}
   199		\]
   200		and bounding the right-hand side by $O(\delta_S + \eps)$ using the two approximations above yields \eqref{eq:qld-sg-cons2} after absorbing $\eps$ into $\delta_S$. The symmetric equivalents follow by the same argument with the register bipartitions interchanged.
   201	\end{proof}

   205	\begin{definition}[The swap unitaries]\label{def:v-swap-unitary}
   206		\uses{lem:qld-4-7, def:generalized-pauli, def:decoding-map}
   207		Define the linear map
   208		\[
   209			V_{\mathrm{A}} = \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ot \bigl(\tau^X(\mathrm{Dec}(g_Z)) \, \tau^Z(\mathrm{Dec}(g_X))\bigr)_{\mathrm{A}''}\;,
   210		\]
   211		where $\tau^X(\cdot)$ and $\tau^Z(\cdot)$ are the generalized Pauli observables acting on $(\C^q)^{\ot M}$; note that the argument of $\tau^X$ is $\mathrm{Dec}(g_Z)$ and the argument of $\tau^Z$ is $\mathrm{Dec}(g_X)$. The map $V_{\mathrm{B}}$, acting on registers $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''$, is defined analogously.
   212	\end{definition}
   213

   215	% definition of the swap unitaries; they are recorded here as a lemma.
   216	\begin{lemma}[Unitarity and conjugation action of the swap unitaries]\label{lem:v-swap-conjugation}
   217		\uses{def:v-swap-unitary, def:tilde-w-observables, def:tilde-m-measurement, def:generalized-pauli, def:indicator-vector, def:bracket}
   218		The maps $V_{\mathrm{A}}$ and $V_{\mathrm{B}}$ of Definition~\ref{def:v-swap-unitary} are unitaries acting on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''$ and $\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'\mathrm{B}''$ respectively, and their conjugation action is exact, as follows. For all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}$, and $\tilde{u} \in \F_q^M$,
   219		\begin{equation}\label{eq:v-swap-obs-conjugation}
   220			V_{\mathrm{A}} \, \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \, V_{\mathrm{A}}^\dagger = \Id_{\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'} \ot \bigl( \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \bigr)_{\mathrm{A}''}
   221			\qquad \text{and} \qquad
   222			V_{\mathrm{B}} \, \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \, V_{\mathrm{B}}^\dagger = \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot \bigl( \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \bigr)_{\mathrm{B}''}\;,
   223		\end{equation}
   224		and for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$, $u \in \F_q^m$, and $a \in \F_q$,
   225		\begin{equation}\label{eq:qld-unitary-6}
   226			V_{\mathrm{B}} \, \tilde{M}^{W,\mathrm{ind}_m(u)}_a \, V_{\mathrm{B}}^\dagger = \Id_{\mathrm{B}\mathrm{B}'} \ot (\tau^W_{[g_h(u)=a]})_{\mathrm{B}''}\;,
   227			\qquad
   228			\tau^W_{[g_h(u)=a]} = \sum_{h \,:\, g_h(u) = a} \tau^W_h\;,
   229		\end{equation}
   230		together with the analogous identity for $V_{\mathrm{A}}$ on registers $\mathrm{A}\mathrm{A}'\mathrm{A}''$.
   231	\end{lemma}

  1666	 The next lemma shows that we can construct local unitaries $V_A,V_B$ from the measurements $\hat{S}$  such that the shared state $\ket{\hat{\psi}}$ is close to $\ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$ for some state $\ket{\aux}$, and the observables $\tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u})$ are mapped to Pauli observables $\tau^W(e_j \tilde{u})$ acting on $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$.   1669	\begin{lemma}
  1670	\label{lem:qld-unitary}
  1671	There exists a function $\delta_\qld(\eps,m,d,q) = O(\delta_S^{1/4} + md/q)$ (where $\delta_S$ is defined in \Cref{lem:qld-4-7}) and unitaries $V_\alice$ acting on registers $\alice \alice' \alice''$ and $V_\bob$ acting on $\bob \bob' \bob''$ such that 
  1672	\begin{enumerate}
  1673		\item There exists a state $\ket{\aux}$ on registers $\alice \alice' \bob \bob'$ such that
  1674		\[
  1675			\left \| V_\alice \otimes V_\bob \ket{\hat{\psi}}_{\alice \alice' \alice'' \bob \bob' \bob''} - \ket{\aux}_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}_{\alice'' \bob''} \right \|^2 \leq \delta_\qld.
  1676		\]
  1677		
  1678		\item For all $W \in \{X,Z\}, h \in \F_q^\nqubits$
  1679		\begin{align*}
  1680			V_\alice \, \Big(M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h \Big)_{\alice} \, V_\alice^\dagger &\approx_{\delta_\qld} \Id_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\tau^W_h)_{\alice''} \\
  1681			 V_\bob \, \Big(M^{(\Pauli,W)}_h  \Big)_{\bob}\, V_\bob^\dagger &\approx_{\delta_\qld} \Id_{\bob \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_h)_{\bob''}
  1682		\end{align*}
  1683		where the $\approx$ statements hold with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}_{\alice'' \bob''}$. 
  1684	\end{enumerate}
  1685	\end{lemma}

  1687	\begin{proof}
  1688	
  1689	Define the linear map
  1690	\[
  1691		V_\alice = \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)))_{\alice ''}\;,
  1692	\]
  1693	where the $\tau^X(\cdot),\tau^Z(\cdot)$ act on $(\C^q)^{\otimes \nqubits}$. (Also note that the argument of $\tau^X$ is $\coded(g_Z)$ and the argument of $\tau^Z$ is $\coded(g_X)$.) We verify the unitarity of $V_\alice$:
  1694	\begin{align*}
  1695		V_\alice V_\alice^\dagger &= \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\alice \alice'} \otimes (\tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) )_{\alice ''} \\
  1696		&= \sum_{g_X,g_Z} (\hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z})_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Id_{\alice ''} \\
  1697		&= \Id_{\alice \alice' \alice''}
  1698	\end{align*}
  1699	where in the first line we used that the measurement $\{ \hat{S}_{g_\xpt,g_\zpt} \}$  is projective and in the second line we used that the $\tau^Z$ and $\tau^X$ observables are self-inverse. The unitary $V_\bob$ is defined analogously.
  1700	
  1701	Let $\{e_j\}_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}}$ denote the self-dual basis for $\F_q$ over $\F_2$ specified in \Cref{sec:subfields}, and let $\tilde{W}^j$ be the observables introduced in~\eqref{eq:def-tildewj}. Conjugating the observable $\tilde{W}^j$ acting on the registers $\alice \alice' \alice''$ by the unitary $V_\alice$ we get
  1702	\begin{align*}
  1703		&V_\alice \, \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \, V_\alice^\dagger \\
  1704	  =& \sum_{g_X, g_Z} (-1)^{\tr( e_j(\coded(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Big ( \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \\
  1705	  &\hspace{24em}\tau^Z(\coded(g_X))^\dagger \tau^X(\coded(g_Z))^\dagger \Big)_{\alice ''} \\
  1706		 =& \sum_{g_X, g_Z} \Big( \hat{S}_{g_X,g_Z}  \Big)_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Big ( \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \Big)_{\alice ''} \\
  1707		 =& \Id_{\alice \alice'} \otimes \Big( \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \Big)_{\alice ''}\;,
  1708	\end{align*}
  1709	where in the third line we used the (anti-)commutation relation
  1710	\[
  1711		\tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) = (-1)^{\tr( e_j(\coded(g_W) \cdot \tilde{u}))} \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \tau^X(\coded(g_Z)) \tau^Z(\coded(g_X)) \;.
  1712	\]

  1714	
  1715	Next, from the self-consistency property of the observables $\tilde{W}^j$ specified in \Cref{lem:qld-construct-the-paulis} we get that for $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
  1716	\[
  1717		\E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \E_{\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits} \bra{\hat{\psi}} \left ( \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \otimes \Id - \Id \otimes \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \right)^\dagger \left ( \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \otimes \Id - \Id \otimes \tilde{W}^j(\tilde{u}) \right) \ket{\hat{\psi}} \leq \delta_S\;,
  1718	\]
  1719	which, since $\tilde{W}^j$ is Hermitian, is equivalent to
  1720	\begin{equation}
  1721	\label{eq:qld-unitary-1}

  1723	\end{equation}
  1724	Let $\ket{\vartheta} = V_\alice \otimes V_\bob \ket{\hat{\psi}}$, and for $W \in \{X,Z\}$ define the operator
  1725	\begin{align*}
  1726		H_W &= \E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \E_{\tilde{u} \in \F_q^\nqubits} \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \otimes \tau^W(e_j \tilde{u}) \\
  1727			&= \E_{j \in \{1,\ldots,t\}} \Big ( \E_{s \in \F_q} \tau^W(e_j s) \otimes \tau^W(e_j s) \Big)^{\otimes \nqubits} \\
  1728			&= \Big ( \E_{s \in \F_q} \tau^W(s) \otimes \tau^W(s) \Big)^{\otimes \nqubits}

  1731	\[

  1733	\]
  1734	for $W \in \{X,Z\}$. 
  1735	
  1736	Observe that
  1737	\begin{align*}
  1738		\E_{s,s'} \tau^X(s) \tau^Z(s') \otimes \tau^X(s) \tau^Z(s') &= \E_{s,s'} \sum_{a,b \in \F_q} (-1)^{\tr(as')} \ketbra{a+s}{a} \otimes (-1)^{\tr(bs')} \ketbra{b+s}{b} \\
  1739		&= \E_{s} \sum_{a\in \F_q} \ketbra{a+s}{a} \otimes \ketbra{a+s}{a} \\

  1741	\end{align*}
  1742	where to go from the first to the second line we used \Cref{lem:cancellation}. This implies that $H_X H_Z = \Big ( \E_{s,s' \in \F_q} \tau^X(s)\tau^Z(s') \otimes \tau^X(s)\tau^Z(s') \Big)^{\otimes \nqubits} = \ketbra{\EPR_q}{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$.
  1743	By the triangle inequality, we have
  1744	\[
  1745		\left \| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \right\| \leq \left \| \ket{\vartheta} - H_X \ket{\vartheta} \right\| + \left \| \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \right\|\;.
  1746	\]
  1747	Note that for $W \in \{X,Z\}$,
  1748	\[
  1749		\left \| \ket{\vartheta} - H_W \ket{\vartheta} \right\|^2 = 1 - 2\bra{\vartheta} H_W \ket{\vartheta} + \bra{\vartheta} H_W^2 \ket{\vartheta} \leq 2 - 2\bra{\vartheta} H_W \ket{\vartheta} \leq \delta_S\;,
  1750	\]
  1751	where in the inequality we used that $H_W \leq \Id$. Furthermore,
  1752	\begin{align*}
  1753		\bra{\vartheta} H_W^2 \ket{\vartheta} &=\| H_W \ket{\vartheta} \|^2\\
  1754		 &= \| \ket{\vartheta} + (H_W - \Id) \ket{\vartheta} \|^2 \\
  1755		 &\geq (\|\ket{\vartheta}\| - \| (H_W - \Id) \ket{\vartheta} \|)^2 \\
  1756		 &\geq (1 - \delta_S)^2 \\
  1757		 &\geq 1 - 2\delta_S\;. 
  1758	\end{align*}
  1759	Therefore 
  1760	\begin{align*}
  1761	2\sqrt{\delta_S} &\geq \left \| H_X \ket{\vartheta} - H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \right\|^2  \\
  1762	&= \bra{\vartheta} H_X^2 \ket{\vartheta} + \bra{\vartheta} H_Z^2 \ket{\vartheta} - 2\bra{\vartheta} H_X H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \\
  1763	&\geq 2 - 4\delta_S - 2\bra{\vartheta} H_X H_Z \ket{\vartheta} \;,

  1765	which implies that 
  1766	\[
  1767		\bra{\vartheta} (\Id_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} \otimes (\proj{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits})_{\alice'' \bob''}) \ket{\vartheta} \geq 1 - 2\delta_S - \sqrt{\delta_S} \;.

  1769	Define the unnormalized state $\ket{\aux_0}$ on the registers $\alice \alice' \bob \bob'$ as
  1770	\[
  1771		\ket{\aux_0}_{\alice \alice' \bob \bob'} = (\bra{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits})_{\alice'' \bob''} \cdot \ket{\vartheta}_{\alice \alice' \alice'' \bob \bob' \bob''}
  1772	\]
  1773	and define the normalized state $\ket{\aux} = \frac{1}{\| \, \ket{\aux_0} \, \|} \ket{\aux_0}$. 
  1774	The inner product between $\ket{\vartheta}$ and $\ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}$ can thus be evaluated as
  1775	\begin{align*}
  1776		\bra{\vartheta} (\ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}) &= \frac{1}{\| \, \ket{\aux_0} \, \|} \cdot \bra{\vartheta} (\ket{\aux_0} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes \nqubits}) \\

  1785	We now establish the second item of the lemma. In what follows, all $\simeq$ and $\approx$ statements hold with respect to the state $\ket{\hat{\psi}}$. From \Cref{lem:qld-win-implications} we have the following implications: for all $W \in \{X,Z\}$ and on average over $u \in \F_q^m$,

   252	\section{The Pauli basis test}
   253	% Paper label sec:qld-game kept for cross-reference fidelity.
   254	\label{sec:qld-game}
   255	
   256	The Pauli basis test is the quantum low individual degree test of Natarajan and Vidick, in the slightly modified form introduced by Natarajan and Wright~\cite{Natarajan2018NEEXP}. Informally, the test certifies that the players share the state $\ket{\mathrm{EPR}_q}^{\ot M}$, where $M = 2^m$. On a question of type $(\mathsf{Pauli}, W)$ with $W \in \{X,Z\}$, a player is expected to measure the generalized Pauli basis POVM $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ of Chapter~\ref{chap:qpbt-algebra} and report the outcome $h$. Most subtests probe limited information about $h$: given a point $u_W \in \F_q^m$, a player is expected to report the evaluation $g_h(u_W)$ of the low-degree encoding $g_h$ of $h$, and for a fixed basis $W$ these probes are checked against each other by the classical low individual degree game of Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}. Consistency \emph{between} the two bases is checked through two-outcome probes: given additionally $r_W \in \F_q$, a player reports $\tr(g_h(u_W)\, r_W) \in \F_2$. The two binary measurements obtained in this way for $W = X$ and $W = Z$ either commute or anticommute, according to the value $\gamma \in \F_2$ of Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value} below. When $\gamma = 0$ the verifier checks commutation directly by asking for both bits simultaneously; when $\gamma = 1$ the verifier checks anticommutation by playing the Magic Square game, using Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.

   899	\subsubsection{The game}
   900	\label{sec:qld-game}
   901	
   902	We start by discussing parameter settings.
   903	The game $\game^\pauli$ is parametrized by a tuple
   904	\[\qldparams = (q,m,d)\;,\] where $q,m,d \in \N$ are integers. 
   905	We sometimes write $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
   906	Pauli basis test on the parameters.
   907	
   908	Informally, the test is meant to certify that the players share a state of the
   909	form $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$, where $M=2^m$.
   910	Its question set includes questions that are axis-parallel/diagonal lines and points in $\F_q^m$,
   911	which are meant to correspond to questions in the classical low-degree test, and questions
   912	of the form $(\Pauli, W)$, for $W \in \{X, Z\}$.
   913	Upon receipt of a question of the latter form, the players are expected to
   914	perform the POVM $\{\tau_h^W\}_{h \in \F_q^{M}}$ and report the outcome $h$ as
   915	their answer.
   916	
   917	The key idea behind the test
   918	is for the provers to encode their outcomes using the \emph{low-degree encoding} from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
   919	Given an outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, the low-degree encoding of~$h$ is the polynomial $g_h:\F_q^m \rightarrow \F_q$.
   920	Rather than asking the provers to always return the entire string~$h$,
   921	many of the subtests in the game $\game^\pauli$ will ``probe'' limited information about~$h$ as follows:
   922	the verifier provides the provers with a string $u_W \in \F_q^m$,
   923	and using this they are expected to evaluate $g_h(u_W) \in \F_q$ and return it to the verifier.
   924	For a fixed value of~$W$, then, the prover's responses to these ``probes'' should be consistent with some low-degree polynomial in the input~$u_W$.
   925	To check this, the verifier can perform the classical low-degree test from Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier}.
   926	This ensures that the prover's responses for the $W = X$ basis are consistent with each other,
   927	as well as their responses for the $W = Z$ basis, although it does not test consistency between the $X$ and $Z$ responses.
   928	
   929	The next set of subtests the verifier performs ensure that the provers' $X$ and $Z$ measurements are consistent with each other.
   930	On the $X$ side, consider the measurement in which the prover performs the $\{\tau_h^X\}$ POVM,
   931	receives outcome $h_X$, and outputs $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$.
   932	For technical reasons that will become clear shortly,
   933	it will be convenient for the prover's measurement to have two outcomes rather than~$q$ outcomes.
   934	To accomplish this, the verifier also provides the prover with an element $r_X \in \F_q$;
   935	given this, the prover should output not $g_{h_X}(u_X) \in \F_q$ but $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$, which is an element of $\F_2$.
   936	Similarly, on the $Z$ side, suppose the prover is provided $r_Z \in \F_q$,
   937	performs $\{\tau_h^Z\}$ to receive $h_Z$, and outputs $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z) \in \F_2$.
   938	Together, these two are a pair of two-outcome measurements, one in the~$X$ basis and one in the~$Z$ basis,
   939	and as it turns out, this pair of measurements either commutes with each other or anticommutes with each other
   940	(this is why we modified the measurements to have only two outcomes).
   941	The key quantity to determine which of these is the case is the following complicated-looking expression:
   942	\begin{equation*}
   943	\gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
   944	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;.
   945	\end{equation*}
   946	If $\gamma = 0$, then these two measurements commute, and if $\gamma = 1$, then these two measurements anticommute
   947	(this fact is established in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-completeness} below).
   948	In the $\gamma = 0$ case, the verifier can check whether these two measurements commute by performing the ``commutation check'',
   949	which asks the provers to simultaneously measure both $\tr(g_{h_X}(u_X) \cdot r_X)$ and $\tr(g_{h_Z}(u_Z) \cdot r_Z)$ and report their values.
   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).
   955	
   956	Together, these give the main subtests for the game $\game^\pauli$.
